analysis.one_liner: Bans big oil company mergers unless the Justice Department finds they promote competition and supplies are guaranteed to independents.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 1999, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten antitrust law for the oil industry. Big vertically integrated oil companies — firms that drill, refine, and sell gasoline — would have been barred from merging with or buying each other unless the Attorney General found the deal would actually promote competition and the company agreed to keep selling crude and fuel to independent refiners and gas station marketers. No senator besides Boxer signed on, the Senate Judiciary Committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent refiners and independent gasoline marketers, who would gain a guaranteed supply of crude and petroleum products and face fewer giant competitors; drivers and communities, who would benefit from more competition at the wholesale and retail level.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent refiners, gas station marketers, drivers

how_it_helps.text: It would block any merger between integrated oil companies unless the Attorney General affirmatively found it would promote competition — shifting the burden onto the companies instead of the government.

It would require merging companies to commit to selling sufficient crude oil and gasoline to independent refiners and independent gas station marketers, with FTC approval, so smaller players could keep competing.

It would let the Attorney General go to federal court to stop deals that violate these conditions, and would require a public report to Congress analyzing each approved merger's effect on competition.

analysis.who_pays: Large integrated oil companies and their shareholders, who would lose the ability to consolidate through mergers and would face new supply obligations to independents; potentially consumers at the margin if some efficiency-creating mergers were blocked.

drawbacks.text: The bill would replace the existing case-by-case antitrust standard with a near-automatic bar on big oil mergers: the Attorney General would have to affirmatively find a merger promotes competition, reversing the normal burden of proof, which could block consolidations that would genuinely benefit consumers through efficiency.

It adds a second layer of government review (both the Attorney General and the FTC must sign off, plus a mandatory supply agreement) on top of existing merger review, which oil companies argued (and some economists agree) slows deals and could reduce industry efficiency.

The requirement that merged companies sell crude and products to independents and marketers at levels sufficient to ensure competition is an ongoing government-set obligation whose terms would need careful enforcement to avoid simply becoming a price-regulation scheme.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits the bill offered a real but narrowly targeted check on oil-industry consolidation, aimed at protecting independent refiners and marketers and, indirectly, consumers. The cost is that it replaced a flexible, evidence-based merger review standard with a near-blanket presumption against big oil mergers, which could have blocked some mergers that genuinely benefit consumers, and it layered a second approval process on top of existing antitrust review. But the bill never advanced far enough for those design questions to be tested; the decisive fact is that it died in committee without a hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Barbara Boxer introduced the Integrated Oil Company Antitrust Act on May 26, 1999.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee — the last action ever taken on the bill.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill never received a committee hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major integrated oil companies are better off: they kept full freedom to merge and consolidate without the proposed pro-competition conditions, while independent refiners and marketers got no protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big oil companies and their shareholders

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate agenda during this period and did not bring the bill up; the Judiciary Committee, chaired by a Republican, never acted on it.

against.name: Major oil companies
against.what_they_did: The industry pursued the merger wave the bill targeted and opposed restrictions on oil-industry consolidation through lobbying and trade groups.

sides.party_line_note: Only one senator, a Democrat, sponsored the bill and no one cosponsored it, so there was never a vote or a visible partisan split to measure.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from merging with or acquiring other integrated companies without a Justice Department finding of pro-competitive effect and an FTC-approved supply commitment to independents — a major new obstacle to the consolidation wave of the era. It was never enacted.

The bill's core purpose was guaranteeing these smaller companies access to crude and petroleum products so they could compete with the majors at the wholesale and retail level. It never became law, so they received no protection.
